operations.specification:
This operation performs a hard deletion of a specific cancellation request line item, operating on the shopping_mall_cancellation_request_items Prisma table. It is used when a cancellation request contains multiple line-level entries (each linked to specific order items or components), and one of those entries must be removed from the request prior to final approval or processing.

The endpoint uses two path parameters: cancellationRequestId identifies the parent cancellation request record from the shopping_mall_cancellation_requests table, and cancellationRequestItemId identifies the concrete line in shopping_mall_cancellation_request_items that belongs to that parent request. The combination ensures that the deletion is scoped correctly and prevents accidental erasure of an item from a different request.

From a business perspective, this deletion will typically be allowed only while the high-level cancellation request is in an editable state (for example, before it has been locked for processing or moved into a final state such as "approved" or "rejected"). The implementing service should enforce such state rules based on the status fields defined in the related Prisma models. Authorization should ensure that only the actor who owns the request (usually the customer or seller who opened it) or an admin with dispute-management permissions can perform this deletion.

The operation does not require a request body, as all the context required to locate the record is provided by the path parameters. On success, the server performs a permanent deletion of the referenced cancellation request item row and returns no response body, signaling that the operation completed successfully via the HTTP status code.
operations.description:
Delete a specific cancellation request item belonging to a particular cancellation request.

This operation targets the shopping_mall_cancellation_request_items table, which stores detailed line-level records for cancellation requests initiated by customers or sellers. Each line typically references a specific order item or related component that the actor wishes to cancel. By providing both cancellationRequestId and cancellationRequestItemId, clients can precisely identify which line within a multi-line cancellation request should be removed before the request is processed further.

In practical workflows, users may adjust their cancellation requests by adding or removing items while the overall request is still under preparation or review. For example, a customer might initially request cancellation of several items and then decide to maintain one of them. This endpoint enables that adjustment by permanently removing the corresponding cancellation request item record from the database.

Security and authorization are critical for this operation. Only the owning account of the cancellation request (for instance, the customer associated with the request) or privileged administrative staff should be able to invoke this API. The backend implementation should validate that the cancellation request is in a modifiable state according to the status and state fields defined on the shopping_mall_cancellation_requests and shopping_mall_cancellation_request_items models. If the request has already progressed to an immutable state, the service should reject the deletion attempt with an appropriate error.

This deletion operation does not return a response body. Instead, successful execution is communicated via the HTTP status code (such as 204 No Content). Related APIs include list and detail retrieval for cancellation requests and items, as well as endpoints for creating and updating cancellation requests before they are finalized.

operations.specification:
This operation searches and retrieves a filtered, paginated list of refund requests from the shopping_mall_refund_requests Prisma table. It is designed for back-office, seller, and customer-facing screens that need to present refund cases with rich filtering, sorting, and pagination capabilities.

The endpoint uses the PATCH method because it accepts a potentially complex search request body instead of simple query parameters. The request body structure is represented by the IShoppingMallRefundRequest.IRequest DTO, which encapsulates filters such as refund request status, creation date range, associated order or payment identifiers, requesting actor, and other domain-specific criteria modeled from the underlying Prisma schema fields. Pagination and sorting controls are also part of this request structure.

The response returns a paginated collection of refund request summaries in a IPageIShoppingMallRefundRequest.ISummary payload. Each summary is based on the shopping_mall_refund_requests table and may include denormalized fields derived from related entities such as orders, payments, or customers, depending on the DTO design. This allows clients to efficiently display lists of refund cases without issuing separate detail queries for every row.

This operation is read-only and does not alter any data in the database. It should be optimized for frequent use, as list and search views for refund management are common in both customer support tools and seller portals. The business logic should enforce any actor-specific visibility rules so that customers only see their own refund requests, sellers see only refund requests affecting their orders or payouts, and admins may see all refund cases.
operations.description:
Search and retrieve a filtered, paginated list of refund requests.

This operation is built on top of the shopping_mall_refund_requests table, which stores high-level refund cases initiated by customers, sellers, or administrators. Each record in this table typically includes references to the related order and payments, current refund status, reason codes, requested amounts, and timestamps that describe the lifecycle of the refund process.

Clients send a structured search payload described by the IShoppingMallRefundRequest.IRequest DTO. This payload may contain various filter fields (such as refund status, creation date range, reason code, associated order identifier, and actor-related information) as well as pagination parameters (page index and page size) and sorting options (for example by created_at or last_status_changed_at). By placing these filters in the request body, the API can support complex querying semantics that would be cumbersome to express in query parameters.

The API responds with a paginated result represented by IPageIShoppingMallRefundRequest.ISummary, where each element provides a summary view of a refund request. Summary objects are optimized for list and dashboard displays, typically containing key fields like refund identifier, linked order number, current status, main reason, total amount, and important timestamps. This design allows UI clients to render large lists efficiently while still offering enough context for users to decide which items to open in detail.

Authorization and visibility rules are applied within the implementation based on the requesting actor. For example, a customer should only see refund requests they initiated, sellers should only see refund requests affecting their orders or payouts, and administrators may be permitted to search across all refund requests in the system. The endpoint itself is modeled as a generic search operation, while finer-grained data access is handled in business logic and database queries.

Errors may be returned if the request body includes invalid filter combinations, unsupported sorting fields, or pagination parameters outside accepted ranges. Related endpoints include detail retrieval for a single refund request, operations for creating new refund requests, and APIs that manage the lifecycle of those requests (such as approval, rejection, or modification).

Retrieve a single refund request record from the shopping_mall_refund_requests table by its primary identifier.

This operation reads a high-level refund case that has been initiated by a customer, seller, or admin after or around delivery. The underlying Prisma model shopping_mall_refund_requests stores the primary business record for a refund case linked to an order and often to a payment, including lifecycle status, requested and approved amounts, currency, reasons, and important timestamps.

The endpoint is intended for detailed inspection of one refund request, typically in customer support, seller back-office, or admin governance UIs. It does not modify any data and is therefore implemented as a GET operation without a request body. The response returns a detailed DTO IShoppingMallRefundRequest that mirrors the Prisma schema fields and includes any necessary relational projections decided at the DTO layer.
operations.description:
Retrieve detailed information about a specific refund request from the shopping mall governance domain.

This operation targets the shopping_mall_refund_requests table, which represents high-level refund cases initiated by customers, sellers, or admins after or around delivery. Each record is a core governance entity that must remain immutable from an audit perspective except for status progression and administrative annotations. The model stores the primary key id, a business-visible request_code, the current lifecycle status, the requested_total_amount and optionally the approved_total_amount, as well as the currency_code and a free-text reason_description providing additional context.

The refund request row is related to several other core entities through foreign keys: shopping_mall_order_id links to the underlying order in shopping_mall_orders; shopping_mall_order_payment_id links to the relevant payment in shopping_mall_order_payments when applicable; shopping_mall_customer_id, shopping_mall_seller_id, and shopping_mall_admin_id connect the refund to the actor who initiated it in shopping_mall_customers, shopping_mall_sellers, or shopping_mall_admins; shopping_mall_refund_request_reason_id references a structured reason in shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons; shopping_mall_cancellation_request_id links to a related cancellation case; and shopping_mall_case_sla_config_id points to SLA rules in shopping_mall_case_sla_configs that govern timelines.

The response includes life-cycle timestamps such as requested_at, decided_at, and completed_at, along with created_at and updated_at for auditing. Because refund requests are sensitive governance records, the actual authorization policy should ensure that only appropriately privileged actors can access particular records. In this specification, the authorizationActors array uses the admin role to represent administrative access to detailed refund governance data.

The operation returns a single IShoppingMallRefundRequest object or an appropriate error when the identifier does not correspond to an existing record.

Create a new refund request record in the shopping_mall_refund_requests table.

This operation allows a relevant authenticated actor (typically a customer, seller, or admin) to initiate a high-level refund case for an order. The underlying Prisma model shopping_mall_refund_requests stores the primary business record for the refund, including the order linkage, the requested monetary amount, currency, lifecycle status, reason code and description, requester actor type, flags such as requires_return, and important timestamps. Related line-level breakdowns are handled separately via shopping_mall_refund_request_items.

The operation must validate business rules such as whether the refund request is still in a modifiable status, whether monetary fields remain consistent with the associated order and payments, and whether the caller has permission to perform the change.

On success, the operation responds with the fully updated refund request resource, ensuring clients receive the canonical representation after all validation and persistence logic have been applied. Before performing the deletion, the implementation must enforce strict business constraints derived from the refund lifecycle. For example, a refund request that has already been fully processed, is tied to completed financial transactions, or is under active dispute may not be eligible for deletion and should instead be protected by governance, auditing, or legal hold requirements. The service should therefore validate the current status of the refund request, any associated financial records, and potential legal or audit flags prior to removal. If the request is not in a deletable state, the operation must return a clear error response indicating why the deletion is not allowed.

This endpoint is typically restricted to administrative or governance-oriented actors with sufficient privileges, because deleting refund requests can impact financial reporting, case tracking, and auditability. Regular customers and sellers would normally cancel or close a refund request through business-state transitions rather than physical removal. Related endpoints include those that create and update refund requests, as well as search and detail retrieval operations that present the existing cases without altering their existence in the database.

The service layer should first verify that the refund request is in a state that allows removal and that there are no legal hold flags, audit obligations, or ongoing dispute processes that require the case to remain stored. If such constraints exist, the operation should fail gracefully, returning an error that indicates the reason, so administrative tools can inform operators that the case must be closed or archived via other mechanisms rather than deleted.

From an authorization standpoint, this endpoint is intended for administrative or governance roles only. Deleting refund requests can have implications for financial reconciliation, compliance reporting, and internal KPIs, so ordinary customers or sellers should not have access to it. In typical workflows, admins might use this operation primarily for correcting erroneous test data in non-production environments or handling very specific operational scenarios under well-defined policies. For day-to-day lifecycle management, other endpoints that update statuses or mark cases as resolved should be preferred over physical removal.

operations.specification:
This operation updates an existing refund request item row in the Prisma table `shopping_mall_refund_request_items` that belongs to a parent refund request tracked in `shopping_mall_refund_requests`. It is a write operation that allows modifying line-level details such as requested refund amounts, target order items or payment components, and other business attributes defined by the schema.

The endpoint models the refund request item as a nested resource under a refund request, addressed by two path parameters: `refundRequestId` to identify the parent `shopping_mall_refund_requests` record and `refundRequestItemId` to identify the specific row in `shopping_mall_refund_request_items`. The request body carries an update DTO that may include only the fields that are allowed to change according to the platform’s business rules.

Because this is an update operation on financial case data, the implementation must enforce strict authorization and state checks. Only authenticated actors such as customers or admins can call the endpoint, and service logic is responsible for verifying that the caller has the right to modify this particular refund request item and that the parent refund request is still in an editable state.
operations.description:
Update an existing refund request item associated with a specific refund request.

This operation works with the `shopping_mall_refund_request_items` Prisma model, which is a subsidiary table that maps refund requests to their detailed monetary impact per order item or payment component. Each record refines the high-level refund case stored in `shopping_mall_refund_requests` with line-level breakdown information. By requiring both `refundRequestId` and `refundRequestItemId` in the path, the API ensures that updates are always scoped to an item that is clearly linked to a given refund request, helping to prevent accidental cross-request modifications.

From a security standpoint, access is limited to authenticated actors such as customers or admins. The underlying service must implement further checks to ensure that the caller is allowed to modify the given refund request item. For example, customers should only be able to update items on refund requests that are associated with their own orders and that are still in a modifiable state, while internal staff such as admins may be allowed to perform adjustments in more states according to policy. Attempts to update items on refund requests that are closed, escalated into disputes, or otherwise locked must result in a validation or conflict error.

Update validation should confirm that the refund request item exists under the provided parent refund request, and that fields being changed (amounts, notes, references to order components, etc.) remain consistent with constraints from `shopping_mall_orders`, `shopping_mall_order_items`, and payment-related tables such as `shopping_mall_order_payments` and `shopping_mall_payment_refunds` where applicable. The DTO type `IShoppingMallRefundRequestItem.IUpdate` encapsulates all updatable properties aligned with the Prisma schema, and the implementation should ignore or reject attempts to modify immutable identifiers.

This endpoint is commonly used in workflows where a user refines or corrects previously submitted refund details, for example adjusting the quantity being refunded for a line item or altering textual explanations before the case is fully processed. It is typically used together with other refund APIs, such as operations for reading refund request details, adding new items, or changing the overall refund request status.

operations.specification:
This operation permanently deletes a specific refund request item associated with a parent refund request in the shoppingMall domain. It operates primarily on the `shopping_mall_refund_request_items` Prisma model, which represents line-level mappings between refund requests and the detailed monetary impact per order item or payment component.

The endpoint is designed for administrative or back-office workflows where an operator needs to remove an individual line from an existing refund request, for example if it was created in error or determined to be invalid during review. Because `shopping_mall_refund_request_items` is a subsidiary entity that belongs to the parent `shopping_mall_refund_requests` record, the path includes both the parent `refundRequestId` and the child `refundRequestItemId` to uniquely and unambiguously identify the target row.

The delete behavior is implemented as a hard deletion of the specified refund request item record. Before performing the deletion, the implementation must validate that the referenced refund request exists, that the refund request item belongs to that refund request, and that the refund request is still in a lifecycle state where structural modification of its items is permitted according to the business policies defined in `shopping_mall_business_policies` and `shopping_mall_policy_versions`. If these validations fail, the operation should respond with appropriate error handling (such as 404 for not found, or 409 for invalid state).
operations.description:
Delete a single refund request item that belongs to a specific refund request in the shoppingMall platform.

This operation targets the `shopping_mall_refund_request_items` table, which is described in the schema as a line-level mapping between refund requests and the specific monetary impact per order item or payment component. Each refund request item captures granular refund details, such as which order item is being refunded and for what amount. The path parameters `refundRequestId` and `refundRequestItemId` are used together to ensure that the item being deleted actually belongs to the specified refund request, preventing accidental cross-request modifications.

From a security and authorization perspective, this endpoint should be restricted to administrative actors or specialized back-office tools, since altering the composition of a refund request after it has been communicated to customers or sellers can have financial and compliance implications. The implementation should perform role and permission checks based on the platform's RBAC configuration (for example, admin roles stored in `shopping_mall_admin_roles` and assignments in `shopping_mall_admin_role_assignments`). Additional guardrails such as legal holds from `shopping_mall_legal_holds` may also prevent deletion when regulatory preservation is required.

In terms of business logic, the deletion is only allowed while the parent refund request is in editable lifecycle states as governed by configurations in `shopping_mall_business_policies`, `shopping_mall_refund_requests`, and their status history in `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories`. If the refund request has already progressed beyond certain thresholds (for example, after payment refunds or chargebacks recorded in `shopping_mall_payment_refunds` or `shopping_mall_payment_chargebacks`), the system should reject the deletion attempt with a conflict response. Related financial aggregates, such as product- or SKU-level rating eligibility in `shopping_mall_review_eligibilities`, may need recalculation when refund items are removed.

Error handling should distinguish between (a) missing refund requests, (b) missing refund request items, and (c) invalid state transitions, returning appropriate HTTP status codes and error payloads. This operation does not return a response body on success; clients should rely on a subsequent retrieval of the parent refund request (for example, an index or detail endpoint on `shopping_mall_refund_requests`) to observe the updated set of items.
operations.summary: Delete a specific refund request item record in the shopping_mall_refund_request_items table.

operations.specification:
This operation retrieves a filtered and paginated list of status history records for a specific refund request in the shoppingMall platform. It operates on the `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories` Prisma model, which stores the chronological record of all status transitions that a refund request has undergone, including timestamps, previous and next statuses, and potentially the actor or system that caused the change.

The endpoint is designed to support both internal operational tools and, when appropriate, customer- or seller-facing UIs that need to display a detailed lifecycle timeline for a refund request. The parent path segment `/refundRequests/{refundRequestId}` ensures that only status history rows associated with the given refund request are queried. The PATCH method is used instead of GET because the request body may contain complex filtering, sorting, and pagination criteria, captured by the `IShoppingMallRefundRequestStatusHistory.IRequest` DTO.

The response returns a paginated collection of status history summaries using the `IPageIShoppingMallRefundRequestStatusHistory.ISummary` type. This summary representation is optimized for timeline or table views, exposing key fields such as status code, transition timestamp, responsible actor, and optional human-readable notes, while omitting heavy or rarely-used columns. Implementations should leverage indexes defined on `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories` (for example, on refund_request_id and created_at) to efficiently support ordering by time and filtering by status.
operations.description:
Retrieve a paginated list of status history entries for a specific refund request, with support for rich filtering and sorting criteria.

This operation focuses on the `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories` table, which the schema describes as the historical record of all status transitions that occurred on a refund request. Each row typically records the previous and new status, the time of transition, the actor or subsystem that initiated the change, and any associated metadata or comments. By scoping the path to `/refundRequests/{refundRequestId}`, the API guarantees that only history entries associated with the identified refund request are returned.

Clients send a structured search payload defined by `IShoppingMallRefundRequestStatusHistory.IRequest` in the request body. This DTO can include fields for pagination (page number, page size), sorting (for example, ascending or descending by transition timestamp), and domain-specific filters such as restricting results to certain status codes, time ranges, or responsible actor types. Since the refund lifecycle is governed by business policies stored in `shopping_mall_business_policies` and `shopping_mall_policy_versions`, these filters allow operators to focus on particular phases of the lifecycle or to investigate specific types of transitions.

Security and authorization considerations depend on the actor. Administrative users, represented in tables such as `shopping_mall_admins` and roles in `shopping_mall_admin_roles`, may be allowed to view full historical details, while customer- or seller-facing views might be restricted or served through separate endpoints. In this specification, the actor is limited to `admin` to reflect a conservative, back-office usage scenario. Implementations should still ensure that legal holds from `shopping_mall_legal_holds` and associated targets in `shopping_mall_legal_hold_targets` are respected when deciding which fields and records can be exposed.

The response body uses the `IPageIShoppingMallRefundRequestStatusHistory.ISummary` structure to deliver a page of status history summary records. This container exposes pagination metadata (such as total count and current page) along with an array of summary entries suitable for UI rendering. Error handling should include clear responses for cases where the parent refund request does not exist, the caller lacks permission to view its history, or the search parameters in the request body are invalid (for example, malformed date ranges or unsupported sort keys).
operations.summary: Search and list status history records for a refund request from the shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories table.

operations.specification:
Retrieve a single detailed status history record for a specific refund request in the shoppingMall domain. This operation is logically associated with the `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories` Prisma model, which stores time-ordered records describing each state transition that a refund request undergoes (for example, from `requested` to `under_review`, then to `approved` or `rejected`). Each history record typically includes fields such as a unique identifier, the parent refund request identifier, the new status value, timestamp of the transition, actor information (who performed or triggered the transition), and any attached notes or reasons.

The endpoint path is `/refundRequests/{refundRequestId}/statusHistories/{statusHistoryId}` and uses the GET method. The `refundRequestId` path parameter identifies the parent refund request whose lifecycle is being inspected, while `statusHistoryId` identifies the particular status transition entry within that refund request's history. The design assumes that `statusHistoryId` is globally unique for status history records. The handler MUST validate that the referenced history entry actually belongs to the specified refund request to prevent cross-reference leakage.

The response returns a single `IShoppingMallRefundRequestStatusHistory` object, which exposes all relevant fields of the underlying `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories` record, including structured status code, timestamps, actor metadata, and any textual reason or comment captured when the status was changed. The operation is read-only and does not modify any state; it may be safely cached where appropriate but must still enforce authorization rules to ensure that only permitted actors (for example, admins or involved sellers/customers depending on business rules) can see sensitive notes or internal statuses.
operations.description:
Fetch a detailed status history record for a specific refund request to understand a particular lifecycle transition event.

This operation focuses on the `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories` table, which is responsible for capturing an append-only audit-style timeline of state changes for refund requests defined in the `shopping_mall_refund_requests` model. Each row in this table typically records the refund request identifier, the status before and after the transition (or at least the resulting status), the exact timestamp when the status changed, and the identity and role of the actor or system component that initiated the change. Descriptive comments or machine-readable reason codes may also be stored to provide context about why the status moved to its new value.

From a security perspective, this endpoint should generally be restricted to administrative or governance actors who are allowed to inspect internal lifecycle details of refund cases, such as operations staff, risk analysts, or dispute resolution teams. Depending on business policy, limited subsets of this information may be exposed to customers or sellers through separate endpoints, but this operation as defined here assumes full-detail retrieval and therefore uses `authorizationActors: ["admin"]`. Implementations must verify that the requesting admin has the required permissions to access refund management data and should ensure that any personally identifiable or sensitive internal annotations are safeguarded according to compliance rules.

The endpoint is tightly coupled to the parent-child relationship between `shopping_mall_refund_requests` and `shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories`. The service must confirm that the given `statusHistoryId` record is attached to the refund request indicated by `refundRequestId`; if not, it SHOULD return a not-found error rather than leaking cross-tenant or cross-case references. Typical error scenarios include non-existent refund requests, non-existent history records, or mismatched pairing between the two identifiers. Related operations that are commonly used together include: listing all history entries for a given refund request (for example, `PATCH /refundRequests/{refundRequestId}/statusHistories`) and high-level refund request detail retrieval (for example, `GET /refundRequests/{refundRequestId}`).
operations.summary: Get a specific status history record for a refund request from shopping_mall_refund_request_status_histories.

operations.specification:
Search and retrieve a filtered, paginated list of refund request reasons configured in the shoppingMall platform. This operation targets the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` Prisma model, which serves as a catalog of structured reason codes and descriptive texts that can be applied to refund and cancellation requests. Typical fields include a unique identifier, a machine-readable code, localized or human-readable labels, categorization fields (e.g., `logistics_issue`, `product_quality`, `payment_problem`), ordering or priority, activation flags, and timestamps.

The endpoint path is `/refundRequestReasons` with HTTP method PATCH, reflecting that the request body carries complex search criteria beyond what is convenient in query parameters. Clients can filter refund request reasons by attributes such as code prefix, active/inactive state, category, or text search in name/description fields. Pagination properties (such as page index and page size) and sort options (such as sort by display order or last updated time) are provided in the request body structure.

The response returns a paginated collection of summary DTOs using the `IPageIShoppingMallRefundRequestReason.ISummary` type. Each list entry exposes fields that are relevant for configuration and UI display, such as the reason code, user-facing label, category, and whether the reason is currently selectable in customer- or seller-facing flows. Because these reasons represent platform configuration rather than sensitive transactional data, this endpoint can typically be accessed by admins responsible for policy configuration and operations staff. The operation is read-only and does not modify any records in `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons`.
operations.description:
Retrieve a paginated list of refund request reasons based on flexible search and filtering criteria.

This operation is built on top of the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` table, which defines the structured reason codes used across cancellation and refund flows in the shoppingMall system. The model usually includes fields such as an internal primary key, an external business code used in APIs and logs, one or more localized display texts, optional grouping or categorization values, a flag indicating whether the reason can be selected by customers or is internal-only, and ordering metadata so that reasons can be presented consistently in user interfaces.

The request body uses the `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason.IRequest` type and allows callers to specify a combination of filters and pagination options. For example, admins can filter by active state to list only currently available reasons, search by code or display text fragments, or restrict results to particular categories (e.g., shipping-related problems versus product defects). Pagination properties control the number of results per page and the offset, while sorting parameters define the ordering of results, such as by display order or last modification timestamp. Validation should ensure that page sizes remain within reasonable bounds to protect performance.

From an authorization standpoint, the list of refund request reasons is typically managed and consumed by administrative and governance tools. As such, this operation is exposed to admin actors via `authorizationActors: ["admin"]`. Implementation should respect any role-based access control configurations to ensure that only permitted administrative users can view or manage the full catalog of reasons. Related operations may include creating or updating refund request reasons through separate configuration endpoints, and using these reason codes in customer- or seller-facing refund and cancellation request creation flows.
operations.summary: Search refund request reasons list from shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons with pagination and filters.

responseBody.description: Paginated collection of refund request reason summaries that match the provided search criteria.

operations.specification:
This operation retrieves a single refund request reason definition from the Prisma table `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons`, identified by its business `reasonCode`. The reason codes represent structured, pre-configured explanations such as "customer changed mind", "item arrived damaged", or "incorrect item shipped" that are used when customers, sellers, or admins create or manage refund and cancellation workflows.

The endpoint is designed as a simple GET detail retrieval by code, optimized for read-only access to the master data that backs refund and cancellation request UX flows. It returns a detailed DTO `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason` that includes all descriptive fields, flags, and metadata defined on the underlying Prisma model (such as localized labels, category/type, and whether the reason is active or usable for specific actors).

The business purpose of this operation is to allow client applications to fetch the full definition of a single refund request reason by its code so that they can display consistent labels and behaviors, validate user selections, and apply appropriate business rules when building or reviewing refund-related cases.
operations.description:
Retrieve detailed information about a single refund request reason record from the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` table by its unique `reasonCode`.

Refund request reasons represent standardized, pre-defined explanations that customers, sellers, or admins can select when creating or updating refund and cancellation requests. The underlying Prisma model `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` typically includes fields such as a human-readable label, a stable machine-readable `reasonCode`, optional grouping/category information (for example, "logistics", "product quality", or "customer preference"), boolean flags indicating whether the reason is currently active, and additional metadata that controls which actors and flows may use the reason.

This endpoint is read-only and is intended to be called by frontend applications or backend services that need to show or validate a particular reason in the context of refund flows. Since this table is master data maintained by governance or operations teams, there is no user-level mutation here; only retrieval by code. API consumers must provide a valid `reasonCode` that exists and is globally unique across all refund request reasons.

If the specified `reasonCode` does not exist or refers to a disabled reason, the implementation should respond with an appropriate error status (such as HTTP 404 for not found, or 410/422 depending on business policy) and must not expose internal configuration details. This operation is commonly used together with the list/search endpoint for refund request reasons (e.g., a PATCH-based index) and with write operations on refund request entities, where the selected `reasonCode` is persisted as part of a refund or cancellation case.
operations.summary: Get a single refund request reason from `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` by its reasonCode

parameters.name: reasonCode
parameters.description: Unique business identifier code of the target refund request reason (global scope). This code corresponds to the `reasonCode` field on the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` Prisma model and uniquely identifies one standardized refund reason definition across the entire platform.

responseBody.description: Detailed definition of the refund request reason associated with the provided `reasonCode`, including label, category, activation flags, and other configuration metadata derived from `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons`.

operations.name: at

prerequisites.description: A refund request reason configuration must be created in `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` (via POST /shoppingMall/admin/refundRequestReasons) so that a record with the specified `reasonCode` exists and can be retrieved by this GET detail endpoint.

operations.specification:
This operation creates a new refund request reason configuration record in the Prisma table `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons`. Governance or operations administrators use this endpoint to onboard additional standardized reasons that can be selected when customers, sellers, or admins initiate refund or cancellation requests.

The request body uses the DTO `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason.ICreate`, which encapsulates all fields required to define a new reason, including the machine-readable `reasonCode`, human-readable label(s), optional categorization, actor and flow eligibility flags, and any other settings present on the Prisma model such as activation status or display ordering. The system validates uniqueness constraints (for example, ensuring that `reasonCode` is not duplicated) and applies any business rules defined on the table (such as allowed value ranges or combinations of flags) before persisting the new record.

Upon successful creation, the operation returns the full `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason` DTO, reflecting the newly stored configuration, including any system-generated fields like identifiers or timestamps that the Prisma model defines. This operation is restricted to administrative actors and is designed for low-volume configuration management rather than high-frequency transactional use.
operations.description:
Create a new standardized refund request reason in the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` table, enabling governance and operations teams to expand the catalog of selectable reasons that appear in refund and cancellation flows.

Administrators call this endpoint with a payload described by `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason.ICreate`, providing a unique `reasonCode`, descriptive text, and any additional configuration fields supported by the Prisma model, such as grouping/category, flags that determine whether the reason is visible to specific actors (customers, sellers, admins), and whether the reason is currently active or experimental. The service layer must enforce uniqueness constraints on `reasonCode` and validate that provided flags and relationships align with the platform’s business policies.

This operation is write-sensitive and therefore limited to administrative users via the `authorizationActors` setting. It is expected to be used in conjunction with read-only endpoints that list or retrieve refund request reasons, and with core refund and cancellation workflows that rely on these codes. On success, it returns the created configuration as `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason`; on failure (for example, duplicate `reasonCode` or invalid payload), it should respond with appropriate error statuses and validation messages without partially creating inconsistent configuration records.
operations.summary: Create a new refund request reason record in `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons`

requestBody.description: Refund request reason creation payload containing the unique `reasonCode`, labels, categorization, visibility flags, and other configuration fields required by `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons`.

operations.name: create

operations.specification:
This operation updates an existing refund request reason in the shopping mall platform, operating on the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` Prisma model. The table represents the catalog of structured reason codes that can be associated with refund and cancellation requests across the marketplace. Each record typically includes a unique business identifier such as `reason_code`, a human-readable title, a detailed description, flags indicating whether the reason is available to customers, sellers, or admins, and metadata about whether the reason is active or deprecated.

The endpoint uses the `reasonCode` path parameter to identify the target refund request reason by its unique business code rather than by an internal surrogate identifier. The request body follows the `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason.IUpdate` DTO, which should contain only the updatable fields such as localized labels, descriptions, actor visibility flags, and activation status. Immutable fields like the `reasonCode` itself are supplied exclusively via the path and must not be changed through this operation.

Business logic for this operation must validate that the specified `reasonCode` exists in `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` and that the update does not violate any governance policies defined by related configuration tables such as `shopping_mall_business_policies`, `shopping_mall_case_sla_configs`, or risk and legal hold configurations. For example, reasons that are referenced by active legal holds or critical policy versions may be restricted from deactivation. The operation should return the fully updated `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason` representation so that admin clients can immediately reflect the current state in their UIs.
operations.description:
Update an existing refund request reason identified by its unique reason code within the shopping mall platform.

This operation targets the `shopping_mall_refund_request_reasons` Prisma model, which is described as the catalog of structured reason codes that can be associated with refund and cancellation requests. Each row in this table corresponds to a business-meaningful reason such as "Customer changed mind", "Item damaged", or "Payment issue". The `reasonCode` field exposed as the path parameter is the primary business key used by administrative tooling and workflow engines to reference a specific reason consistently across orders, refunds, disputes, and reporting pipelines.

When an administrator invokes this API, they supply the `reasonCode` in the path and a request body matching `IShoppingMallRefundRequestReason.IUpdate`. The update DTO should include only mutable fields from the underlying Prisma schema, such as the human-readable title, long-form description, flags indicating whether the reason is available for customers or sellers to select, and whether the reason is currently active. Fields that define the identity of the reason, including the `reasonCode` itself, must not be changed by this operation and are instead used purely as lookup keys.

From a security and authorization perspective, this operation is restricted to admin actors, reflected by the `authorizationActor` value `"admin"`. The request body will follow the IShoppingMallDispute.ICreate DTO, which encapsulates all fields that a client is allowed to set at dispute creation time, such as the disputeCode if client-generated, external reference identifiers, initial severity or type selection, and human-readable description. On success, the API returns the created dispute as an IShoppingMallDispute object that mirrors the shopping_mall_disputes model including resolved references to customer, seller, admin, and related transactional entities where applicable. operations.description:
Create a new dispute case in the ShoppingMall dispute management subsystem.

This endpoint operates on the shopping_mall_disputes table, which stores high-level dispute entities representing serious conflicts involving orders, refunds, chargebacks, or policy violations. The Prisma schema for shopping_mall_disputes typically includes a stable unique disputeCode used in external URLs and communication, references to related orders or payments, fields for dispute type and severity, as well as lifecycle status fields. When a client invokes this API, only fields explicitly allowed in the IShoppingMallDispute.ICreate DTO are accepted, while internal audit and lifecycle attributes are managed by the backend.

From a security perspective, this operation must be restricted to authenticated actors that are allowed to initiate disputes, such as customers, sellers, or admins. For this reason, the authorizationActors array includes "customer", "seller", and "admin", indicating that any of these authenticated platform user types can call the endpoint while fine-grained permissions (e.g., whether a seller may escalate a specific order) are checked against the authenticated principal and underlying Prisma relations.

The relationship between shopping_mall_disputes and subsidiary tables like shopping_mall_dispute_events, shopping_mall_dispute_parties, and shopping_mall_dispute_evidences is important for implementation but transparent to the API consumer. The provider is expected to create an initial event row that records the opening of the dispute and to maintain consistency with SLA-related tables such as shopping_mall_case_sla_configs and shopping_mall_case_sla_violations indirectly. If validations fail—for example, because the referenced order or payment does not exist, the dispute type is not allowed for the current actor, or a duplicate open dispute already exists for the same subject—the endpoint must respond with appropriate error codes explaining why the dispute could not be opened.

Clients typically call this operation from UI flows such as "Report a problem with this order" or "Dispute this chargeback". After creation, additional endpoints dedicated to adding dispute events, evidences, or moderation decisions will evolve the dispute over time; this creation endpoint itself is idempotent with respect to the server-generated primary key but not necessarily with respect to the business key, so implementers may enforce uniqueness constraints around disputeCode or a composite of subject identifiers to avoid duplicate open disputes.

The Prisma model for shopping_mall_disputes is expected to define this code field with a unique constraint so that the backend can reliably look up the dispute row using the provided value.

The request body uses the IShoppingMallDispute.IUpdate DTO, which contains only the subset of fields that can be updated after creation. operations.description:
Update an existing dispute identified by disputeCode in the shopping_mall_disputes table.

This endpoint targets the shopping_mall_disputes Prisma model, which defines the persistent schema for high-level disputes on the ShoppingMall platform. The disputeCode path parameter is a business-level identifier exposed to users in URLs and notifications; it must correspond to a unique code column on the shopping_mall_disputes table so that the implementation can perform an efficient lookup. Using a code instead of an internal UUID in the path keeps URLs stable and user-friendly across customer, seller, and admin UIs.

The request body follows the IShoppingMallDispute.IUpdate DTO and is designed around the Prisma schema comments that distinguish mutable and immutable fields. Typical mutable fields include display-oriented metadata like dispute title, categorization and reason classification, internal or external notes, and flags controlling visibility to different actors. Fields representing primary relationships, such as the linked order, payment, or account, as well as initial creation metadata, are generally immutable and therefore excluded from the update DTO. The backend must validate that all attempted updates are consistent with both the schema constraints and business rules defined in policy tables like shopping_mall_business_policies and shopping_mall_policy_versions.

Security-wise, this operation is restricted to authenticated platform users of types customer, seller, or admin, expressed here as authorizationActors ["customer", "seller", "admin"]. Actual permission checks—such as ensuring that only the dispute owner or an authorized admin can modify specific fields—are performed in the provider layer using the authenticated principal and related records such as shopping_mall_dispute_parties. If the disputeCode does not correspond to an existing dispute, the service must return a not-found error. If the requested update violates status-based rules—for example, attempting to modify a closed dispute that has been locked due to legal holds recorded in shopping_mall_legal_holds and shopping_mall_legal_hold_targets—an appropriate validation error should be generated and no change persisted.

This endpoint is typically used by client-side flows like editing dispute details or applying administrative reclassification. It complements other write-oriented dispute APIs (e.g., adding events or evidences) by focusing on the core dispute header record in shopping_mall_disputes.

operations.specification:
This operation permanently deletes a single dispute record identified by its globally unique business code from the Prisma table `shopping_mall_disputes`. It is intended for use by administrative actors performing governance and risk management tasks when a dispute case has been fully resolved, archived elsewhere, or opened in error and must be removed from the active dispute portfolio.

The operation accepts the dispute's business identifier as a path parameter, using `disputeCode` rather than an internal UUID to match the domain requirement that disputes be referenced by their external case code in administrative tools and audit reports. The Prisma `shopping_mall_disputes` model is expected to define this code as a unique field (for example, via a `@@unique([code])` constraint), allowing safe lookup and deletion by code. No request body is required, and the endpoint either completes successfully with no content or returns an appropriate error if the code does not exist or cannot be deleted due to business constraints such as legal holds.

From a business perspective, deletion of disputes should be tightly controlled. Typical implementations will enforce checks in the service layer to ensure the dispute is in a deletable state (for example, closed and not under legal hold) and that the caller has sufficient administrative privileges. All related subsidiary entities such as parties, events, and evidences stored in tables like `shopping_mall_dispute_parties`, `shopping_mall_dispute_events`, and `shopping_mall_dispute_evidences` should be handled according to the platform's referential integrity policy (for example, cascading deletion or prior archival).
operations.description:
Delete a single dispute record from the `shopping_mall_disputes` table using its business-visible dispute code.

This operation targets the primary dispute entity that encapsulates high-severity conflicts involving orders, refunds, chargebacks, or policy violations. The underlying Prisma model `shopping_mall_disputes` is described as a primary table for platform-level disputes that tie together complex financial and policy-related issues. By deleting a dispute via this endpoint, the system removes the core dispute record that other subsidiary tables such as `shopping_mall_dispute_parties`, `shopping_mall_dispute_events`, and `shopping_mall_dispute_evidences` reference through foreign keys.

From a security and governance standpoint, only high-privilege administrative actors should be allowed to execute this operation. The `authorizationActors` is therefore set to `["admin"]`, indicating that only admin-type users authenticated by the platform may call this endpoint. Service-level authorization logic should additionally verify that the dispute is eligible for deletion, for example ensuring that there is no active legal hold in `shopping_mall_legal_holds` or related tables that would require the data to be preserved for compliance or investigation.

In terms of validation and business rules, the service implementation must first resolve the dispute by its `disputeCode` path parameter, which corresponds to a globally unique business identifier (for example, a human-readable case code) rather than an internal UUID. If the dispute does not exist, the operation should respond with a 404-style error. If the dispute exists but cannot be deleted due to policy, the implementation should return an appropriate error such as 409 conflict along with a message describing why the deletion is blocked (for example, open chargeback, unresolved refund, or legal hold).

Related API operations include listing and retrieving disputes for analysis and case handling, as well as endpoints for managing associated parties, events, and evidence. This deletion operation should be used sparingly and usually only after the dispute lifecycle has fully completed and the platform has either archived or exported any information required for long-term reporting and compliance.

operations.specification:
This operation retrieves a filtered, paginated collection of parties associated with a specific dispute from the Prisma table `shopping_mall_dispute_parties`. It is used primarily by administrative and risk management tools to inspect who is involved in a given dispute—including customers, sellers, admins, or external entities—and what roles they play in the conflict lifecycle.

The endpoint is implemented as `PATCH /disputes/{disputeCode}/parties` to support complex search and filtering semantics in the request body while still being a read-only analytical operation. The path parameter `disputeCode` identifies the parent dispute in the `shopping_mall_disputes` table using its globally unique business code, while the request body DTO `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.IRequest` carries optional filters such as party type, role, creation date ranges, and pagination and sorting options. The response returns a paginated summary collection `IPageIShoppingMallDisputeParty.ISummary` tailored for list views in administrative consoles.

Internally, the service implementation will resolve the parent dispute using the provided `disputeCode`, join to the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` table via the dispute's primary key, and apply the supplied filters and ordering. Because `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` is documented as a subsidiary table representing entities that participate in a dispute, this operation never creates or mutates parties; it is strictly read-only and does not alter the underlying data. Only authorized admin actors may access this endpoint, as dispute participation details may contain sensitive information about customers, sellers, or external organizations involved in risk or compliance cases.
operations.description:
Retrieve a filtered and paginated list of parties for a specific dispute from the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` table.

This operation provides administrative users with insight into who participates in a given dispute case, including customers, sellers, admins, and potentially external entities such as payment providers or logistics partners. The underlying Prisma model `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` is described as a subsidiary table that links disputes from `shopping_mall_disputes` to the actors involved, capturing roles and relationships that are important for case handling and decision making.

The `disputeCode` path parameter specifies which dispute's parties are being queried. This code is a globally unique business identifier on the `shopping_mall_disputes` table (for example, a human-readable case code used in operations dashboards), ensuring that the correct parent dispute context is applied. After resolving the parent dispute, the service queries `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` for all matching records, applying filters from the `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.IRequest` request body. Typical filters may include party type (customer, seller, admin, external), role within the dispute (complainant, respondent, observer), creation or update time ranges, and free-text search on display names or reference identifiers.

The response body returns a paginated collection `IPageIShoppingMallDisputeParty.ISummary`, which is optimized for list displays in administrative consoles and case management tools. Each summary item should contain essential fields such as party type, role, identifiers, and key timestamps, without unnecessarily loading deeply nested relationships. Pagination metadata (such as page number, page size, and total count) are included to support scalable navigation through large dispute cases with many involved parties.

Security-wise, this endpoint is restricted to administrative actors, reflected by `authorizationActors: ["admin"]`. Implementers should ensure that appropriate authentication and authorization checks are enforced and that sensitive information about parties is only exposed to users with sufficient privileges. This operation is typically used together with other dispute endpoints, such as detail retrieval for the dispute header itself and timelines of dispute events, to provide a comprehensive view of complex cases.

responseBody.description: Paginated list of dispute party summaries associated with the specified dispute and matching the given search criteria.

operations.specification:
This operation retrieves a single dispute party associated with a specific dispute from the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma model. It uses the dispute's business identifier code as a stable, human-readable path parameter and the dispute party's UUID identifier to locate the exact party record.

The endpoint is designed for administrative or governance tools that need to inspect who is involved in a dispute, such as customers, sellers, admins, or external entities. It should resolve the dispute by its unique `code` field from the `shopping_mall_disputes` table (or equivalent) and then ensure that the requested party belongs to that dispute based on a foreign key like `shopping_mall_dispute_id` on `shopping_mall_dispute_parties`.

The response structure is modeled as `IShoppingMallDisputeParty`, the primary DTO representing a dispute party. It is expected to include core attributes such as the party type (customer, seller, admin, external), identifiers of the underlying actor, and metadata about their role in the dispute. No request body is required, and the endpoint is read-only.

Authorization is restricted to administrative actors (e.g., governance, risk, or support staff), represented by the `admin` actor. The underlying implementation must ensure that the dispute and party exist, that the party belongs to the dispute referenced by `disputeCode`, and that any sensitive personal or financial data is handled in accordance with platform governance and compliance requirements.
operations.description:
Retrieve a specific dispute party record for a given dispute using the dispute's business code and the party's UUID identifier.

This operation reads from the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma model, which stores entities that participate in a dispute, such as customers, sellers, admins, or external entities. It expects that the parent dispute is represented in the `shopping_mall_disputes` model with a globally unique business `code`, and that each party row includes a foreign key pointing to that dispute. The path parameter `disputeCode` is used to identify the dispute in a human-friendly, business-oriented way, while `disputePartyId` is a UUID that uniquely identifies the party record within the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` table.

From a security and permissions standpoint, this endpoint is intended for administrative and governance tools rather than for end users. The `authorizationActors` array is therefore set to `["admin"]`, ensuring that only authenticated admin actors can call this operation. The actual authorization layer should verify that the calling admin has the appropriate role and permission to view dispute and party information, particularly if sensitive details about customers, sellers, or external entities are exposed.

In terms of business logic, the implementation must ensure that the party being retrieved actually belongs to the dispute identified by `disputeCode`. This typically involves first resolving the dispute by its code in `shopping_mall_disputes`, then querying `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` for a row with the matching dispute primary key and the provided `disputePartyId`. If either the dispute or party is not found, or if the party does not belong to that dispute, the system should return a not-found error.

Error handling should clearly distinguish between invalid identifiers (malformed UUID), missing resources (dispute or party not found), and authorization failures. Related APIs include listing all parties for a dispute and viewing the dispute itself, which together give admins a complete picture of the dispute context, participants, and timeline based on the `shopping_mall_disputes` and `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` models.

The specific dispute party must be created before it can be fetched by disputePartyId; POST /shoppingMall/admin/disputes/{disputeCode}/parties creates a party row linked to the dispute.

operations.specification:
This operation creates a new dispute party record within the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma model, associating a given actor (such as a customer, seller, admin, or external entity) with a specific dispute. It uses the dispute's business `code` from the `shopping_mall_disputes` table to identify the parent dispute and a request body of type `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.ICreate` to describe the new party.

The request DTO `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.ICreate` is expected to contain all fields necessary to create a valid dispute party, such as the party type, references to the underlying actor (e.g., customer ID, seller ID, or external reference), and any role-specific metadata. The implementation must map the `disputeCode` from the URL to the internal dispute primary key and then create a new row in `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` that is correctly linked to that dispute.

The operation is intended for internal admin tools and governance workflows, where staff need to add new participants to an existing dispute—for example, adding a new investigating admin, an external payment provider contact, or a legal representative. Authorization is limited to the `admin` actor, and all necessary validation rules, such as ensuring that the dispute exists and that the same party is not duplicated improperly, must be enforced.
operations.description:
Create a new dispute party for an existing dispute by specifying the dispute via its business code and providing party details in the request body.

This operation writes to the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma model, which captures entities that participate in disputes tracked by the `shopping_mall_disputes` model. The path parameter `disputeCode` identifies the parent dispute via its globally unique business `code`. The service must first resolve this code to the dispute's primary key. The request body of type `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.ICreate` then supplies all necessary fields to define the new party, including its type (such as customer, seller, admin, or external entity), references to the underlying actor, and any descriptive metadata required by platform governance rules.

Security and authorization are critical because this operation changes the set of participants in a dispute. Only admin actors are allowed to call this endpoint, as indicated by `authorizationActors: ["admin"]`. The actual implementation should verify that the admin has sufficient privileges—for example, specific roles that allow dispute management or risk case handling—and should record audit logs in tables such as `shopping_mall_admin_audit_logs` if present in the broader schema.

Business logic must ensure data integrity by validating that the dispute identified by `disputeCode` exists and is in a state where adding new parties is allowed. It should also confirm that the combination of dispute and party being added does not violate uniqueness constraints in `shopping_mall_dispute_parties`, such as preventing duplicate party entries when the same actor and role already exist for the dispute. On success, the operation returns the newly created party as `IShoppingMallDisputeParty`, reflecting the persisted state.

Error handling should differentiate between invalid dispute codes, disputes that do not allow modifications due to lifecycle state, validation errors in the provided party data, and authorization failures. This operation is commonly used alongside APIs that retrieve or list dispute parties, allowing admins to view and adjust the full set of dispute participants within the governance workflows.

operations.specification:
This operation updates an existing dispute party record associated with a particular dispute in the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma table. The endpoint is designed for administrative or governance tooling that needs to adjust information about a participant in a dispute case, such as changing their role, contact details snapshot, or status within the dispute lifecycle.

The underlying Prisma model `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` is a subsidiary table that links a dispute case (from `shopping_mall_disputes`) to concrete participating entities (customers, sellers, admins, or external organizations). The business semantics typically include fields describing the party type, references to the corresponding actor entity, and metadata about their involvement in the dispute. This operation focuses on modifying those mutable attributes while keeping core identity keys (the dispute code and the dispute party identifier) immutable and expressed through path parameters.

The API consumes an `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.IUpdate` DTO, which encapsulates only the updatable fields of a dispute party, excluding identifiers such as `disputeCode` and `disputePartyId` that come from the URL. The response returns the updated `IShoppingMallDisputeParty` representation so that admin tools can immediately reflect the latest party configuration and ensure data consistency in dispute management interfaces.
operations.description:
Update an existing dispute party associated with a specific dispute, allowing governance or operations staff to adjust party attributes without changing its identity.

This operation targets the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma table, which serves as a subsidiary entity under `shopping_mall_disputes`. Each row typically represents a participating entity in a dispute case, such as a customer, seller, administrator, or external counterparty. The table commonly stores the link back to the parent dispute, the classification of the party, and context data needed for handling the dispute. Administrative users may need to correct or enrich this information over time as more facts are gathered or as roles change during the resolution process.

Security-wise, the endpoint is restricted to administrative actors because modifying dispute participants directly impacts compliance, risk handling, and legal posture. The `authorizationActors` configuration therefore uses `"admin"`, assuming that only admin accounts, with appropriate role-based access within the shopping mall platform, can invoke this mutation. Business logic behind this operation should validate that the target dispute exists, that the specified party belongs to that dispute, and that the update does not violate governance rules such as locked disputes or legal holds.

The request body follows the `IShoppingMallDisputeParty.IUpdate` contract, which includes only fields that are semantically safe to change after creation, such as display labels, role or stance within the dispute, contact or representation metadata, and internal flags relevant to case handling. Identity fields and foreign keys are not part of the DTO and are instead taken from the path parameters `{disputeCode}` and `{disputePartyId}`. This prevents inconsistent updates and ensures that the composite relationship between the dispute and its parties remains stable.

On success, the operation returns the full `IShoppingMallDisputeParty` resource, reflecting all persisted changes and any derived fields or computed flags that the backend may populate. Client applications, such as admin consoles or risk management dashboards, are expected to call this endpoint when editing a dispute party and then refresh their local state using the returned representation. In case of invalid input, missing records, or business rule violations (for example, attempting to modify a dispute party in a closed or legally held dispute), the implementation should return appropriate error responses following the platform’s standardized error handling conventions.
operations.summary: Update a dispute party record in the shopping_mall_dispute_parties table for a given dispute.

operations.specification:
This operation permanently removes a dispute party record from the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma table for a given dispute. It is intended for administrative use in scenarios where a previously registered participant was added in error, is no longer relevant to the case, or needs to be removed following specific governance policies.

The `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` table functions as a subsidiary entity that associates disputes from `shopping_mall_disputes` with the various actors involved. Removing a row from this table breaks that association and effectively removes the party from further consideration in the dispute workflow. The operation identifies the target record using a human-readable dispute code and a technical dispute party identifier, both provided as path parameters.

This endpoint does not accept a request body because all information necessary to identify the record is captured by `{disputeCode}` and `{disputePartyId}`. On successful deletion, the operation does not return a resource body; clients are expected to rely on the HTTP status code to confirm the outcome. If the platform prefers to return a small confirmation object instead, that can be modeled separately, but by default this specification assumes a body-less success response to keep the API surface focused.
operations.description:
Remove a specific dispute party from a dispute so that the party is no longer tracked as a participant in the dispute’s lifecycle.

The underlying storage for this operation is the `shopping_mall_dispute_parties` Prisma table, where each entry links an actor to a dispute in the `shopping_mall_disputes` table. From a business standpoint, removing a dispute party means that the platform will no longer show this party in dispute views, timelines, or role assignments. This is typically necessary only in carefully controlled situations, such as correcting data entry mistakes or aligning the system of record with external legal guidance.

Because altering dispute participants has compliance implications, access to this endpoint is restricted to administrative actors, represented by `authorizationActors: ["admin"]`. Implementation logic should additionally enforce any internal governance rules, such as refusing to delete parties from disputes that are locked due to legal holds in `shopping_mall_legal_holds`, or requiring that at least one primary party remain associated with the dispute.

The path parameters `{disputeCode}` and `{disputePartyId}` uniquely identify the dispute and party combination. The backend must validate that the specified party actually belongs to the dispute identified by `disputeCode` before performing the deletion. If no matching record exists, or if business rules prohibit the removal (for instance, when the party has attached evidence records or is referenced by dispute events), the operation should return an appropriate error with explanatory messaging according to the platform’s error contract.

On success, the endpoint responds with an HTTP status indicating that the party has been removed from the dispute. Clients such as admin consoles or risk dashboards should then refresh the dispute detail view and no longer list the removed party among participants. Any derived aggregates, such as counts of parties per dispute, should be updated by the backend as part of the same transaction or through background processing, depending on the system’s design.
operations.summary: Delete a dispute party record from the shopping_mall_dispute_parties table for a given dispute.

The dispute party identified by {disputePartyId} must have been created for the dispute via POST /shoppingMall/admin/disputes/{disputeCode}/parties before it can be removed with DELETE /shoppingMall/admin/disputes/{disputeCode}/parties/{disputePartyId}.

operations.specification:
This operation searches and retrieves a filtered, paginated list of dispute events associated with a specific dispute in the shoppingMall platform. It is primarily associated with the `shopping_mall_dispute_events` Prisma table, which records the timeline of actions, status changes, comments, and system decisions that occur during the lifecycle of a dispute represented by the `shopping_mall_disputes` table.

The endpoint uses a PATCH method on `/disputes/{disputeCode}/events` to support complex search criteria in the request body while remaining read-only. The client specifies the target dispute using its business-friendly unique `disputeCode` path parameter (a code column with a unique constraint in `shopping_mall_disputes`) rather than a low-level internal identifier. The request body type `IShoppingMallDisputeEvent.IRequest` carries optional filters such as event types, creation time ranges, involved party types, and pagination and sorting options. The response returns a paginated collection of dispute event summary records using `IPageIShoppingMallDisputeEvent.ISummary`.

From a business standpoint, this operation enables back-office agents, risk analysts, and other authorized users to review the full history of how a dispute has evolved. It is used in combination with the dispute header retrieval and detailed dispute views to provide a complete picture of case handling and to satisfy auditability and governance requirements.
operations.description:
Retrieve a filtered, paginated list of dispute events associated with a single dispute identified by its business dispute code.

This operation works with the `shopping_mall_dispute_events` Prisma model, which stores the chronological event timeline for disputes defined in the `shopping_mall_disputes` table. Each event typically records when a particular action occurred (such as dispute creation, evidence submission, escalation, or resolution), who performed it (customer, seller, admin, or automated system), and the resulting status or state change. The path parameter `disputeCode` corresponds to the business-level code field on `shopping_mall_disputes` that is marked with a unique constraint, making it safe to use as a stable identifier in URLs from administration consoles and internal tools.

The request body of type `IShoppingMallDisputeEvent.IRequest` allows callers to specify detailed search criteria and pagination controls. For example, callers can filter dispute events by a range of event timestamps, event categories or types, event sources (system vs. human actors), or references to related entities such as payments or orders where supported by the schema. Pagination fields in the request body control the size and page of the result set, and sorting instructions allow ordering by event time, creation time, or importance. These flexible search capabilities are important for operational teams who need to quickly zoom in on key moments in the dispute lifecycle.

Security-wise, this endpoint should be restricted to back-office and governance actors such as admins or specialized dispute-handling staff, since dispute events can contain sensitive operational notes, internal decisions, and risk-related information that must not be exposed to general customers or sellers. The `authorizationActors` property is therefore set to `["admin"]`, and additional fine-grained authorization based on admin roles and permissions from RBAC tables (for example `shopping_mall_admin_roles` and `shopping_mall_admin_role_assignments`) should be enforced in the service layer. Events are always read-only in this context; creation and updates of dispute events are handled by internal workflows and other operations, not by this search endpoint.

This operation is typically used together with the dispute header retrieval operation (for the `shopping_mall_disputes` table) and any dispute evidence listing operations (for `shopping_mall_dispute_evidences`) to provide a complete view of the dispute. Clients will first fetch the dispute header to understand high-level details, then call this endpoint to load the full event timeline for inspection, analysis, or reporting purposes.
operations.summary: Search dispute events for a specific dispute (shopping_mall_dispute_events) with pagination and filters
